Lam Research stock faces supply squeeze after record quarter
sum: Lam Research reported record fiscal first-quarter revenue of 8.22 billion US dollars for the September quarter on October 21, while adjusted earnings per share reached 2.20 US dollars. The figures exceeded analyst estimates, according to 24/7 Wall St.

Chief Executive Tim Archer attributed the quarter's performance to strong demand from artificial intelligence and increasing chip complexity. The company makes etch and deposition equipment used in semiconductor manufacturing, leaving revenue closely tied to customer fab construction and production plans.

Lam Research guided for December-quarter revenue of 8.6 billion US dollars, plus or minus 400 million US dollars, and adjusted earnings per share of 2.33 US dollars, plus or minus 0.15 US dollars. Chief Financial Officer Doug Bettinger said the revenue outlook would have been higher without near-term supply-chain constraints.

Management did not quantify the revenue affected by the bottleneck. Bettinger said some orders that cannot ship in the December quarter should move into the March quarter. Cleanroom availability is another constraint as customers bring new facilities online, while Lam also expects China's contribution to decline from 35 percent of September-quarter revenue in the December period.

The supply issue changes the near-term investment case without removing the longer-term demand signal. Lam Research expects global wafer-fabrication-equipment spending to exceed 200 billion US dollars in calendar 2027, although management said unconstrained demand would be higher. Archer said the company had visibility through 2028 but needed more time to refine the outlook around cleanroom schedules and supply availability.

For investors, the December quarter will show whether the constraint is mainly a timing issue or a more persistent limit on shipments. A rapid catch-up would support the view that demand remains stronger than near-term delivery capacity; prolonged bottlenecks would keep execution risk elevated even with a healthy order environment.

Lam Research Stock Is 45% Below Its High. How Deep Have Past Drops Gone?
sum: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Shares of Lam Research (LRCX) have dropped 40% or more in three of the 15 market shocks it has traded through since 2007, meaning a decline of that size has happened before. The stock lost 24.7% in the month to October 26, 2026, compared with a 0.8% dip for the S&P 500, even as Lam reported its fifth straight quarter of record revenue. At $237.50 on October 26, the shares were already 45.1% below their June 30 high. Buyers stepping in now may be counting on Lam holding up in a downturn and on those record sales lasting. So how far has Lam fallen when the whole market turned, and for how long?

Lam usually drops further than the broader market during downturns. The deepest decline across those 15 shocks occurred during the 2008-2009 financial crisis, when the stock fell 66% while the S&P 500 lost 53%. The performance gap widened during the 2022 inflation shock, as Lam slid 56% against a 24% decline for the index. The third drop of 40% or more happened in the 2020 COVID-19 crash, when Lam lost 44% compared with a 34% fall for the index. Across all 15 shocks, Lam recorded an average decline of 22.8%, against the 15.8% average drop for the S&P 500.

The shares typically recover within months, though some rebounds take longer. Measured from the lowest close in each shock, the stock took a median of 2.4 months to return to its previous high. Three of those recoveries lasted more than a year. The longest period followed the summer 2007 credit crunch and required 80.3 months, while the rebound after the 2008-2009 crisis took 23.2 months.

So far, the company’s record sales are lasting. Revenue for the September quarter, fiscal Q1 2027, reached $8.22 billion. That figure was up 54.4% from a year earlier, and management said systems revenue in memory rose 120% over the same period. Operating margin came in at 40.0%, up from 34.4% a year earlier.

Over the last twelve months, Lam’s operating margin was 37.0%. That is the highest level across the 40 quarter ends from fiscal Q2 2017 to now, up from 19.7% at the start of that period. The company also finished September with $7.44 billion in cash and short-term investments, held against $3.74 billion of debt.

sum: Bank of America is telling clients that the fourth quarter belongs to a select group of semiconductor names, even as the sector's most prominent AI bellwether delivered blockbuster results that left the market unmoved.

In a note to clients on Wednesday, BofA semiconductor analyst Vivek Arya named Nvidia (NVDA), Intel (INTC), Micron Technology (MU), Marvell Technology (MRVL) and Lam Research (LRCX) as his top five chip picks heading into the final stretch of the year. The call comes as the bank substantially raised its long-term outlook for AI infrastructure spending, lifting its estimate for the AI data center systems market to $2.2 trillion by 2030, up from a prior forecast of $1.8 trillion and implying roughly 40% annual growth.

The timing is no accident. Arya pointed to historical data showing that the fourth and first calendar quarters have been the two strongest seasonal periods for owning semiconductor stocks. Between 2010 and 2025, chip equities delivered median outperformance of 300 to 500 basis points relative to the S&P 500 during those quarters.

Valuation is another pillar of the thesis. The PHLX Semiconductor Index trades at about 21 times forward earnings, roughly 12% below its median multiple of 24 times since ChatGPT launched. That discount stands against projected earnings growth of more than 40%, according to the bank's analysis.

"The virtuous flywheel of agentic tool adoption by consumers and enterprises, competition between public and private AI labs, and limited chip supply will likely keep AI spending robust for the next several years," Arya wrote. By the bank's estimate, a single agent workflow can generate 10 to 1,000 times more tokens than a chat exchange. He added that any slowdown in frontier model development or addition of safety guardrails would likely increase, rather than reduce, computing requirements, shifting more demand toward faster-growing inference workloads.

The bank's forecast for combined capital expenditure by major U.S. and Chinese cloud providers now sits at roughly $1 trillion for 2026, about double last year's level, climbing to $1.4 trillion by 2027 and reaching $2 trillion to $3 trillion by the end of the decade.

items.t: Where Lam Research Stock Is Most Exposed
sum: The chip equipment maker is firing on all cylinders, but a slowdown in its single largest market presents a risk that investors shouldn't ignore.

It's hard to find a flaw in the Lam Research (LRCX) story right now. The stock has delivered a 320% return over the last 12 months, results are hitting record levels, and the narrative of an accelerating AI-driven semiconductor demand environment appears robust. But for a stock priced this richly, the most important question is what could go wrong. The answer may lie in one number: the company's revenue concentration in China.

In its most recent quarter, Lam Research derived 34% of its total revenue from China. A single country accounting for more than a third of sales is a significant concentration for any company. The concern, however, extends beyond the size of the exposure to its direction. That 34% figure is down from 35% in the prior quarter. More pointedly, management was direct on its earnings call, stating, "We expect that China revenue in the June quarter will decline from these levels." This isn't a hypothetical risk; it's a stated expectation from the company itself.

A slowdown in one geography might seem manageable for a global leader, but it creates a challenge for a stock with such high expectations. Lam Research currently trades at a price-to-sales multiple of 22.4, a figure well above its own 10-year high of 12.3. A valuation this high suggests the market is pricing in strong execution and continued high growth. When a segment that represents a third of your business is guided to shrink, it puts pressure on the rest of the company to accelerate just to keep the overall growth story intact. This trend is also happening alongside another cautionary signal: management noted that customer down payments are now at "the lowest level we've seen in nearly 4 years," a metric they acknowledge is correlated with customers in the China region.

A continued slowdown in China presents a risk to the top-line growth that underpins Lam's premium valuation. Investors must look past one or two quarters of softer revenue. The more critical question is whether the market will continue to pay a historically high multiple for a company whose largest single market is showing signs of deceleration.
